subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: hiding the mistake and hoping it goes unnoticed [Pitfall]
passage:
Friday, evening.
The audit finished today. In March I typed the wrong tax rate into forty invoices. I didn't tell anyone. I opened each invoice and quietly changed it, no note, no reason. It took an evening, and I felt clever.
Today the auditors flagged edits with no explanation. Arnab, my manager, called me in. "Did you change these?" I said, "Yes, I fixed a typo." That wasn't the whole truth and Arnab knew it.
"The wrong rate," Arnab said, "I'd have fixed in a day. This I can't ignore." He didn't shout. That was worse.
I don't know if I'll get the same access again. I wish I'd walked to Arnab's desk in March.
— Hansa

qa.q: How many invoices did Hansa change quietly?
What was Hansa feeling while talking to Arnab?
qa.a: Hansa was ashamed and afraid, giving a half-truth and finding Arnab's quiet reaction worse than shouting.

qa.q: What could Hansa do now to begin rebuilding trust with Arnab?
qa.a: Hansa could give Arnab the full story, share a written account of every edit and offer to follow any check the team sets.

qa.q: How might Arnab have seen the hidden edits compared with the original mistake?
qa.a: Arnab saw the original mistake as easy to fix in a day, but the silent edits as a breach of trust that could not be ignored.

grounding: The diary shows an employee who quietly patches an error and says nothing, so that when an audit finds it later the concealment harms trust more than the mistake.

subtopic: Recovering from a major work mistake
subtype: Approach: hiding the mistake and hoping it goes unnoticed [Pitfall]
passage:
In the cooperative bank's branch at Wai, Swati noticed her mistake on a Thursday: a farmer's loan entered as 1,80,000 instead of 1,08,000. The farmer had signed for the smaller amount and received it. Nobody else had seen.
She corrected the figure late that evening under an old adjustment code and said nothing to Thomas, the branch manager. It felt small, she was new, and she did not want to be known as the girl who made errors.
In November the district auditor came. He found the adjustment with no note, no approval and her login. Thomas was called in first. 'Why didn't you tell me?' he asked her afterwards, not angry, just tired. 'A typing mistake I could have signed off in five minutes. Now the auditor wants to check every file you've touched.'

qa.q: What amount did the farmer sign for?
Why did Swati say nothing, and what was she worried about?
qa.a: She was new and worried about looking careless, embarrassed to be known as someone who made errors.

qa.q: What could Swati have done instead on that Thursday?
qa.a: She could have told Thomas and corrected it with his approval and a note, turning it into a five-minute sign-off.

qa.q: What is it like for Thomas when the auditor calls him in?
qa.a: Thomas is tired and disappointed, now answering for a hidden change in his branch that he could easily have approved.

grounding: It shows an employee quietly fixing an error and saying nothing, so when an audit finds it the concealment damages trust more than the mistake.
